question.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,3)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}-4x+5}+3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-3)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-4x+5}+3-3)}^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-4x+5})^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{x}^{2}-4x+5 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+{x}^{2}-4x+5 \\  & =2{x}^{2}-8x+9.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=4x-8 & =0 \\ 4x & =8 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=4>0.$ Therefore, $x=2$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=2$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(2)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S\,(2)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(2)^{2}-8(2)+9} \\  & =\sqrt{8-16+9} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
